title: Item Response Theory (IRT): Models, Difficulty, Discrimination, Guessing, Invariance
summary: IRT models; item difficulty; item discrimination; guessing parameter; item characteristic curve; invariance assumption; advantages over CTT.
objectives: Explain item parameters a, b, c.
revision: IRT: item-level model. a = discrimination, b = difficulty, c = guessing. ICC plots P(correct) vs θ. Parameters invariant across samples. CTT vs IRT: test vs item level.
traps: IRT parameters are invariant across samples (advantage over CTT).

notes.t: A family of measurement models that relate the probability of a correct response to a person's latent trait level and item characteristics.
The ICC plots the probability of a correct response (y-axis) against the person's ability level θ (x-axis). The curve is S-shaped (ogive).

r: Ability level at which probability of correct response = 0.50
How well the item distinguishes high- from low-ability
Lower asymptote — probability of guessing correctly

notes.t: Item parameters are invariant across populations, and person parameters are invariant across items (within the model). This is a key advantage over CTT.

Worked example: Item with b = 0 (difficulty). A person with θ = 0 has 50% probability of answering correctly. A person with θ = +1 (above average) has higher probability; θ = −1 (below average) has lower probability.
IRT item parameters (a = discrimination, b = difficulty, c = guessing) and the invariance property are frequently tested.

r: Test scores or estimated true scores

notes.t: OCR-extracted from source page 113: Table comparing CTT and IRT models (Hambleton and Jones, 1993). Key distinction: CTT statistics are sample-dependent while IRT statistics are sample-independent (if the model fits test data). IRT typically requires larger samples (500+) for stable parameter estimation.
